The locality-guide agent has completed its survey of **Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)** and written a locality entry (`loc_001`) to your project. Here is its full report, plus an important note at the end:

---

## Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

**Formed:** 10 December 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties | **County seat:** Somerset | **State-land state**

### Key findings

- **Vital records are sparse.** Civil registration operated only during 1853–1862 and 1874–1878, with poor compliance. Statewide registration didn't begin until 1911. For births and deaths, use church records, census mortality schedules, and tax lists as substitutes.
- **Marriage bonds are the strongest vital series**, running from 1799. FamilySearch has digitized 1799–1871; marriage bonds survived the courthouse disasters.
- **Two courthouse disasters** (1838 and 1871) destroyed some early records — treat records near those years as potentially incomplete.
- **Probate and will books** from 1801–1929 are digitized on FamilySearch.

### Top record types for 1840–1880
| Record Type | Where to Find |
|---|---|
| Marriage bonds (1799–1871) | FamilySearch (digitized) |
| Will books (1801–1929) | FamilySearch (digitized) |
| Church records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian) | FamilySearch (partial); Pulaski Co. Historical Society |
| Federal census (1840–1880) + mortality schedules | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| County deed books | Pulaski Co. Courthouse; KDLA microfilm |
| Tax lists | Ancestry; KDLA |
| Civil War service records & pension files | NARA; Fold3 |
| Newspapers | Kentucky Historical Society; Newspapers.com; Chronicling America |

### Critical repositories
- **Pulaski County Historical Society** — surname vertical files and church records not replicated online
- **Kentucky Dept. for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort** — microfilmed county records
- **Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort** — grants, warrants, surveys, patents (metes-and-bounds state; do NOT search BLM GLO)
- **NARA** — federal military records; both Union AND Confederate service records apply (border-state complexity)

---

## ⚠️ Greenup County and Boyd County Still Needed

The agent noted that **Greenup County and Boyd County** (northeastern Kentucky, on or near the Ohio River) were not covered in this session. Each has a distinct geography, record-keeping history, and jurisdiction context from south-central Pulaski County. You can continue the session with that agent to survey them, or ask me to launch a new survey for those two counties.

# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 10 December 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky (state-land state)
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by tools during this survey — consult U.S. federal census schedules directly (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880)
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence farming, tobacco), timber; south-central Kentucky hill country
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Scots-Irish and English settlers descending from Virginia-era migration; small enslaved African-American population
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian were the largest denominations in Kentucky per the FamilySearch Wiki Kentucky Church Records page; Catholic presence was minimal in south-central rural Kentucky
- **Key historical events:** Civil War divided Kentucky loyalties; the county seat of Somerset was the site of the Battle of Mill Springs (January 1862) nearby in Wayne/Pulaski county area

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County was formed 10 December 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties. Boundaries were stable throughout the 1840–1880 target period.
- Records predating 1799 are held under Lincoln or Green County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates and levels:** County-level registration operated during 1853–1862, 1874–1878, and 1892–1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration did not begin until 1911 (general compliance achieved by 1917). Source: [Kentucky Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **What exists for 1840–1880:** County-level birth and death records from 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 (partial compliance only); marriage bonds and licenses from county formation (1799) onward — these are the most reliably complete vital record series.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502); KDLA holds microfilmed copies; FamilySearch has digitized marriage bonds/consent forms 1799–1871.
- **Gaps:** The 1838 and 1871 courthouse disasters destroyed some records. Civil registration was absent or incomplete for the majority of births and deaths in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian), family bibles, cemetery inscriptions, and newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian were the largest Kentucky denominations in this era. Catholic presence in south-central rural Kentucky was minimal per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, church minutes
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed records from many Kentucky congregations); Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort); Filson Historical Society (Louisville, primarily Louisville-area records); Pulaski County Historical Society (most comprehensive local church record collection); Southern Baptist Historical Library (Nashville) for Baptist records; denominational conference archives for Methodist; Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia) for Presbyterian records. Source: [Kentucky Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records).
- **Online:** FamilySearch collections include *Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995* (index and images, incomplete), *Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960* (index only), *Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979* (index only), and *Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970* (index only).
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — Pulaski County fully within the target period. 1850 onward lists individuals by name; 1840 lists only the head of household.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census date and are a partial substitute for missing death registrations.
- **State census:** Kentucky did not conduct a state census series equivalent to some other states.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and online at FamilySearch, Ancestry, and related platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships, court orders
- **Date range:** Probate from 1801; court records from 1799
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA (microfilmed copies); FamilySearch has digitized early will books 1801–1929
- **Note:** The 1838 and 1871 courthouse disasters may have created gaps in probate and court series. When a person died testate (left a will), search will books; intestate (no will), search administration files.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Kentucky is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds land grants, original warrants, surveys, and patents. Grant periods relevant to 1840–1880 include Old Kentucky Grants (1793–1856), Kentucky Land Warrants (1816–1873), and Grants South of Green River (1797–1866). Source: [Kentucky Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Types:** Deeds (county), grants and patents (Kentucky Land Office), tax lists
- **Date range:** County deed books from 1799
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (deeds); Kentucky Land Office and Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort) for grants; Ancestry and FamilySearch have Kentucky land grant images online.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) — Pulaski County had both Union and Confederate enlistees; post-war veterans would be subject to pension filings
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812 and Mexican War era), Civil War draft registrations, compiled military service records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and Atlanta regional facility for southeastern states); Fold3 (subscription, online service and pension records); Kentucky State Archives for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Numerous rural church cemeteries and family burial grounds throughout Pulaski County
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — coverage is volunteer-driven and incomplete for rural cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for older rural church cemeteries are held by the individual congregation or the Pulaski County Historical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Somerset-area newspapers existed during this period; specific titles and date ranges were not returned by tools in this survey — contact the Pulaski County Historical Society or Kentucky Historical Society for holdings
- **Where held:** Kentucky Historical Society; some holdings on Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), local news

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Pulaski County is an inland south-central Kentucky county. Significant international immigration was minimal in this period. The population was predominantly native-born of earlier colonial-era settler descent.
- **Relevant records:** Naturalization papers (filed in county circuit court, pre-1906); for any foreign-born residents, passenger arrival lists at NARA and Ancestry
- **Note:** Passenger lists record all passengers including infants and children traveling with families — examine the full manifest when researching family groups.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax lists (real and personal property); poll tax
- **Date range:** From county formation; county tax lists survive for much of the 19th century
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA; Ancestry has Kentucky tax list collections
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for missing census years and can place a person in the county in off-census years.

### Other record types
- **County histories:** Published local histories from the late 19th and early 20th centuries often contain biographical sketches of founding families and transcriptions of early records — check WorldCat and the Kentucky Historical Society.
- **Occupational records:** Agricultural census schedules (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) list farm production and livestock by household — useful for economic profiling.
- **Enslaved persons records:** Slave schedules in the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses list enslaved individuals by age, sex, and physical description (no names) under the enslavers' households.

## Repository guide

| FamilySearch | Marriage bonds/consent forms (1799–1871); will books (1801–1929); Kentucky Church Records (1818–1995, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings (1839–1960); Kentucky Marriages (1785–1979); Kentucky Deaths and Burials (1843–1970); federal censuses; land grant images | Free |
| Ancestry | County tax lists; census records; vital record indexes; land grants | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions (volunteer coverage, incomplete for rural areas) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspaper issues | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Some Kentucky newspapers, free | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military records, pension files, naturalization records | Free finding aids; some digital, some physical |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (limited for KY state-land state) | Free |

The online collections listed above are drawn from the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pulaski County and Kentucky, fetched by constructed URL. Researchers should search FamilySearch.org directly (catalog and records search) for current digitization status.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, Somerset, KY | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from 1799 | In-person; some records microfilmed at KDLA |
| Pulaski County Historical Society | Surname vertical files; church records; newspaper obituaries | In-person or written inquiry |
| Kentucky Dept. for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 vital records | In-person or online finding aids |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, land records, newspapers, county histories | In-person; some online |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; some online via FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| NARA, Washington DC / Atlanta | Federal military service/pension; naturalization | In-person or written request; many online |
| Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville | Baptist church records | Written inquiry |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church records | Written inquiry or online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- The majority of Pulaski County circuit court and county court minute books
- Most local church congregation registers (only a portion have been microfilmed)
- Sexton records for rural church cemeteries
- Local newspaper runs not included in Newspapers.com or Chronicling America

Kentucky is a state-land state — land grants are at the Kentucky Land Office in Frankfort, not the BLM GLO; county deed books run from county formation (1799).

The Pulaski County Historical Society maintains surname vertical files and the most comprehensive local collection of church records and newspaper obituaries — contact them before assuming a record is lost.

# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 10 December 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky (state-land state)
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by tools during this survey — consult U.S. federal census schedules directly (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880)
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence farming, tobacco), timber; south-central Kentucky hill country
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Scots-Irish and English settlers descending from Virginia-era migration; small enslaved African-American population
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian were the largest denominations in Kentucky per the FamilySearch Wiki Kentucky Church Records page; Catholic presence was minimal in south-central rural Kentucky
- **Key historical events:** Civil War divided Kentucky loyalties; the county seat of Somerset was the site of the Battle of Mill Springs (January 1862) nearby in Wayne/Pulaski county area

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County was formed 10 December 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties. Boundaries were stable throughout the 1840–1880 target period.
- Records predating 1799 are held under Lincoln or Green County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates and levels:** County-level registration operated during 1853–1862, 1874–1878, and 1892–1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration did not begin until 1911 (general compliance achieved by 1917). Source: [Kentucky Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **What exists for 1840–1880:** County-level birth and death records from 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 (partial compliance only); marriage bonds and licenses from county formation (1799) onward — these are the most reliably complete vital record series.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502); KDLA holds microfilmed copies; FamilySearch has digitized marriage bonds/consent forms 1799–1871.
- **Gaps:** The 1838 and 1871 courthouse disasters destroyed some records. Civil registration was absent or incomplete for the majority of births and deaths in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian), family bibles, cemetery inscriptions, and newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian were the largest Kentucky denominations in this era. Catholic presence in south-central rural Kentucky was minimal per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, church minutes
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed records from many Kentucky congregations); Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort); Filson Historical Society (Louisville, primarily Louisville-area records); Pulaski County Historical Society (most comprehensive local church record collection); Southern Baptist Historical Library (Nashville) for Baptist records; denominational conference archives for Methodist; Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia) for Presbyterian records. Source: [Kentucky Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records).
- **Online:** FamilySearch collections include *Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995* (index and images, incomplete), *Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960* (index only), *Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979* (index only), and *Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970* (index only).
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — Pulaski County fully within the target period. 1850 onward lists individuals by name; 1840 lists only the head of household.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census date and are a partial substitute for missing death registrations.
- **State census:** Kentucky did not conduct a state census series equivalent to some other states.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and online at FamilySearch, Ancestry, and related platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships, court orders
- **Date range:** Probate from 1801; court records from 1799
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA (microfilmed copies); FamilySearch has digitized early will books 1801–1929
- **Note:** The 1838 and 1871 courthouse disasters may have created gaps in probate and court series. When a person died testate (left a will), search will books; intestate (no will), search administration files.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Kentucky is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds land grants, original warrants, surveys, and patents. Grant periods relevant to 1840–1880 include Old Kentucky Grants (1793–1856), Kentucky Land Warrants (1816–1873), and Grants South of Green River (1797–1866). Source: [Kentucky Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Types:** Deeds (county), grants and patents (Kentucky Land Office), tax lists
- **Date range:** County deed books from 1799
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (deeds); Kentucky Land Office and Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort) for grants; Ancestry and FamilySearch have Kentucky land grant images online.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) — Pulaski County had both Union and Confederate enlistees; post-war veterans would be subject to pension filings
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812 and Mexican War era), Civil War draft registrations, compiled military service records
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and Atlanta regional facility for southeastern states); Fold3 (subscription, online service and pension records); Kentucky State Archives for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Numerous rural church cemeteries and family burial grounds throughout Pulaski County
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — coverage is volunteer-driven and incomplete for rural cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for older rural church cemeteries are held by the individual congregation or the Pulaski County Historical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Somerset-area newspapers existed during this period; specific titles and date ranges were not returned by tools in this survey — contact the Pulaski County Historical Society or Kentucky Historical Society for holdings
- **Where held:** Kentucky Historical Society; some holdings on Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), local news

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Pulaski County is an inland south-central Kentucky county. Significant international immigration was minimal in this period. The population was predominantly native-born of earlier colonial-era settler descent.
- **Relevant records:** Naturalization papers (filed in county circuit court, pre-1906); for any foreign-born residents, passenger arrival lists at NARA and Ancestry
- **Note:** Passenger lists record all passengers including infants and children traveling with families — examine the full manifest when researching family groups.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax lists (real and personal property); poll tax
- **Date range:** From county formation; county tax lists survive for much of the 19th century
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA; Ancestry has Kentucky tax list collections
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for missing census years and can place a person in the county in off-census years.

### Other record types
- **County histories:** Published local histories from the late 19th and early 20th centuries often contain biographical sketches of founding families and transcriptions of early records — check WorldCat and the Kentucky Historical Society.
- **Occupational records:** Agricultural census schedules (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) list farm production and livestock by household — useful for economic profiling.
- **Enslaved persons records:** Slave schedules in the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses list enslaved individuals by age, sex, and physical description (no names) under the enslavers' households.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Marriage bonds/consent forms (1799–1871); will books (1801–1929); Kentucky Church Records (1818–1995, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings (1839–1960); Kentucky Marriages (1785–1979); Kentucky Deaths and Burials (1843–1970); federal censuses; land grant images | Free |
| Ancestry | County tax lists; census records; vital record indexes; land grants | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions (volunteer coverage, incomplete for rural areas) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspaper issues | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Some Kentucky newspapers, free | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military records, pension files, naturalization records | Free finding aids; some digital, some physical |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (limited for KY state-land state) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `wiki_place_page` tools returned empty standardPlace fields throughout this survey and produced no usable digitization data. The online collections listed above are drawn from the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pulaski County and Kentucky, fetched by constructed URL. Researchers should search FamilySearch.org directly (catalog and records search) for current digitization status.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, Somerset, KY | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from 1799 | In-person; some records microfilmed at KDLA |
| Pulaski County Historical Society | Surname vertical files; church records; newspaper obituaries | In-person or written inquiry |
| Kentucky Dept. for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 vital records | In-person or online finding aids |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, land records, newspapers, county histories | In-person; some online |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; some online via FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| NARA, Washington DC / Atlanta | Federal military service/pension; naturalization | In-person or written request; many online |
| Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville | Baptist church records | Written inquiry |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church records | Written inquiry or online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- The majority of Pulaski County circuit court and county court minute books
- Most local church congregation registers (only a portion have been microfilmed)
- Sexton records for rural church cemeteries
- Local newspaper runs not included in Newspapers.com or Chronicling America
- Original land survey plats (held at Kentucky Land Office)

## Known record losses
- **1838 courthouse disaster:** Some early Pulaski County records destroyed. Exact scope unknown; records predating or near this date should be treated as potentially incomplete.
- **1871 courthouse disaster:** A second loss destroyed additional records. Marriage bonds 1799–1871 are available on FamilySearch, suggesting at least marriage records survived or were reconstructed before the 1871 event, but other series may have gaps.
- **Substitute sources:** Tax lists, church records, census records, and probate filings in neighboring-county courts can partially compensate.

## Research tips
- **Vital records gap:** For births and deaths 1840–1880, civil registration was sporadic at the county level. Church records and census mortality schedules are your primary sources. Consult [Kentucky Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **Marriage records are the strongest vital record series:** Marriage bonds and licenses run from 1799 and have survived relatively well. FamilySearch has digitized the 1799–1871 series.
- **Record losses in 1838 and 1871:** Work around the gaps by using tax lists (place in county by year), census records, and church records.
- **State-land state:** Do not look for Pulaski County land in the BLM GLO federal patent database — go to the Kentucky Land Office and the county deed books. Consult [Kentucky Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **The Pulaski County Historical Society is essential:** Their surname vertical files and church record collection are not replicated online. Contact them early in your research.
- **Civil War context:** Kentucky was a border state with divided loyalties. Pulaski County men served in both Union and Confederate forces. Search both NARA's compiled military service records (Union and Confederate captured records) and Kentucky's own state archives for militia records.
- **Neighboring counties:** The neighboring-county table was not returned by the wiki home page tool in this survey session. Researchers should check Wayne, Russell, Lincoln, Rockcastle, Laurel, and McCreary counties for families near the borders — deeds, probate, and church records frequently cross county lines.
- **Agricultural census schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — list farm output by household. Useful for distinguishing families with the same name.
- **Enslaved persons:** Slave schedules (1850 and 1860) list enslaved individuals under the enslaver's household — no names, but age and sex are given. Freedom Bureau records begin 1865 and may document formerly enslaved individuals.
- **FamilySearch catalog:** The catalog search returned 0 hits for Pulaski County and also for Kentucky during this survey session — this is a tool resolution issue, not confirmed absence of microfilm. Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly at familysearch.org/search/catalog for Pulaski County holdings.

## Alabama Region, circa 1800 — Archives & Record Repositories

Researching an ancestor in the Alabama region around 1800 means working across **three overlapping jurisdictions**: the area was **Mississippi Territory** in 1800, became **Alabama Territory** in 1817, and then the **State of Alabama** in 1819. Records follow the jurisdiction that created them.

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery) | Territorial censuses from 1801, 1805, and 1808; early county tax lists |
| **FamilySearch** (Mississippi Territory collections) | Land and court records beginning 1799 |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm copies of French and Spanish colonial church registers and land grants |
| **Library of Congress** | Additional microfilm of colonial Mobile records |
| **Archives in Seville & Aix-en-Provence** | Original French/Spanish colonial church registers and land grants for the Mobile area, going back to 1702 |

### Important Caveats for 1800

- **No civil birth or death registration** existed anywhere in the region in 1800.
- **The 1800 federal census does not survive** for Alabama.
- The research strategy therefore centers on **land entries, territorial tax lists**, and (for Mobile) **colonial-era church records**.
- Three browse-only digitized volumes on FamilySearch cover territorial court and land records for 1799–1820, but **none can be searched by name** — they must be examined page by page.

### Recommended Starting Points

1. Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) at ADAH
2. Mississippi Territory land and court records on FamilySearch (1799+)
3. Colonial Mobile church registers if your ancestor was in the Mobile district

The guide has been saved to the project for future reference. The next step would be building a research plan targeting your specific ancestor through these available sources.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (c. 1795-1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory created 1817 from the eastern half of Mississippi Territory; Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819. In 1800, the entire region was Mississippi Territory (organized 1798).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Natchez was the territorial capital; St. Stephens became the seat of the Alabama district by ~1817.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), then Alabama Territory (1817-1819).
- **Population during period:** Sparse; approximately 9,000 free persons in the Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory per the 1810 federal census.

Here is the locality guide returned by the subagent:

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (c. 1787–1810)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, covering present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio became the first state carved from that territory on **1 March 1803**.
- **Administrative centers:** Marietta (Washington County seat, 1788) and Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat, 1790) were the two principal nodes for the entire territory in the 1790 period.
- **Population:** Extremely sparse Euro-American settlement before 1800, with substantial Native American populations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami). Active military conflict through the Treaty of Greenville (1795) severely limited civilian record-keeping.

---

## Boundary Changes — The Critical Factor

The jurisdictional picture was entirely fluid for 1790 Ohio:

| Year | Change |
|------|--------|
| 1787 | Northwest Territory established — no county subdivisions yet |
| **1788** | **Washington County organized** — covered all of eastern Ohio (east of the Scioto River and beyond). All records from Marietta and surroundings are Washington County records. |
| **1790** | **Hamilton County organized** — covered southwestern Ohio, including Cincinnati. |
| 1796+ | Additional counties carved rapidly (Adams, Clermont, Fairfield, Trumbull, etc.) |
| 1803 | Ohio statehood; territorial government dissolved |

**Practical rule:** An event in "Ohio" in 1790 was recorded — if at all — under Washington County or Hamilton County territorial court records, *not* under any later county covering the same modern geography. Always identify which 1788–1803 county held the location before searching.

### Three Concurrent Land Survey Districts (geographic, not temporal)

Ohio was not surveyed uniformly. Three distinct land systems operated simultaneously, each with records in *different* repositories:

1. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): Reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans; metes-and-bounds survey. Warrants and grants are at the **Virginia State Library**.
2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Different grid system. Records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland**.
3. **Federal tracts** (Seven Ranges, U.S. Military District, etc.): Administered by the federal government; patents searchable free at **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov).

You must know the approximate location within Ohio before you can identify the correct land repository.

---

## Available Records

### Vital Records
- **No civil registration existed in 1790** or at statehood (1803). Statewide vital registration came much later.
- **Marriage exception:** "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (FamilySearch collection 1803785; 1.5M records) begins at the territory's founding and is indexed — the primary civil marriage source for this era.
- **Deaths:** County death records do not begin until 1840 (FamilySearch collection 1417891).
- **Pre-registration alternative for births/deaths:** Church records only.

### Church Records
- Thin coverage for 1787–1800. Circuit riders served most communities; formal congregations were few.
- FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (collection 2246917; 678,234 records) is available online.
- Denominational archives hold originals: Presbyterian Historical Society, United Methodist Archives, various Quaker meeting archives.

### Census Records
- **1790 federal census:** Incomplete or missing for Ohio/Northwest Territory due to frontier conditions and active warfare. **Do not rely on it.**
- **1800 federal census:** First reliable enumeration for most Ohio locations; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- No confirmed territorial census for pre-1803 Ohio.

### Land Records — Most Important Source for 1790
- **FamilySearch:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187; 234,567 records; indexed/name-searchable).
- **Territorial land records 1788–1799:** FamilySearch digitized volume 005112233 (51 images; **0% name-indexed, browse-only** — must be examined image by image).
- **BLM GLO:** Federal patents searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Virginia Military District warrants:** Virginia State Library (physical/microfilm).

### Tax Records — Key Substitute for Missing 1790 Census
- Washington County tax records begin **1799** (FamilySearch volume 005112240; 73 images; 12% indexed — mostly browse-only).
- "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (FamilySearch collection 1987542; 345,890 records).

### Probate and Court Records
- Washington County territorial court records begin 1788; Hamilton County 1790.
- Held at the **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** (not yet identified as indexed/digitized on FamilySearch for the territorial era).

### Military Records
- Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) and Revolutionary War veterans settling in the Virginia Military District.
- National Archives (NARA) for pension files and bounty land warrants; Fold3 online.
- Virginia Military District bounty land warrants: Virginia State Library.

### Newspaper Records
- *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* (Cincinnati, founded 1793) — first newspaper in the territory.
- Limited digitization of 1790s papers. Newspapers.com has some coverage.

---

## Known Record Gaps

- 1790 federal census essentially absent for Ohio.
- Most pre-1800 church records were never formally organized (itinerant preachers' registers, often lost).
- Early territorial court minutes are physical-only at the Ohio History Connection.
- County formation was rapid — records created under Washington County (1788) for areas later carved into new counties **remained with Washington County**, not transferred.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Always determine the 1788–1803 county first.** Modern county boundaries are irrelevant for 1790 research.
2. **Land records are the primary anchor for 1790.** Start with "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" and BLM GLO; browse the 1788–1799 territorial land volume image by image.
3. **Virginia Military District requires a Virginia search** — land warrants originated in Virginia, not Ohio.
4. **Connecticut Western Reserve requires the Western Reserve Historical Society** — not the Ohio History Connection or BLM.
5. **Tax lists substitute for the absent 1790 census** — the Washington County tax list begins 1799 (12% indexed; browse the rest).
6. **The marriage collection reaches back to 1789** — check FamilySearch collection 1803785 even though no statewide registration existed.
7. **19th-century county histories are essential** — they frequently transcribed territorial court minutes, early land entries, and pioneer biographies that may be the only surviving record of 1790s events. Search WorldCat for Washington County and Hamilton County, Ohio histories.
8. **Search adjoining states too.** Families arriving in Ohio in the 1780s–1790s came through Pennsylvania and Virginia; their earlier records are there. For southwestern Ohio families, Kentucky records across the Ohio River may also apply.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1789+; Land Records 1787–1840; Church Records; Tax Records 1800–1850; browse-only territorial volumes | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Territorial court records 1788–1803; state archives | In-person / Ohio Memory |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrants & grants | In-person / some digitized |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person / research inquiries |
| NARA, Washington DC | Military pensions, bounty land warrants, territorial records | In-person / Fold3 |
| Ancestry | 1800 federal census; other indexed collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Pioneer cemetery records | Free |

---

The central challenge of 1790 Ohio research is that the state didn't yet exist, counties formed rapidly with shifting borders, and civil infrastructure was almost entirely absent. **Land records and the 1800 census are the primary documentary anchors**, supplemented by the 1789+ county marriage records and whatever church records survive from frontier congregations. If you can identify an approximate settlement location within Ohio, the next step would be pinning down the correct 1788–1803 county and land survey district to target the right repositories.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (c. 1787–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, covering present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. Ohio became the first state carved from that territory on 1 March 1803.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County seat, 1788); Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat, 1790). These were the two principal administrative nodes for the entire territory in the 1790 period.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory of the United States (1787–1803), administered under federal territorial law before statehood.
- **Population during period:** Population data for Ohio specifically in the 1780s–1790s is not available from the FamilySearch population tool at this resolution; the territory's American-settler population was extremely sparse before 1800. Wikipedia notes the region had substantial Native American populations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) and only scattered Euro-American settlement until after the Treaty of Greenville (1795).
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrison economy, and early land speculation. The region was an active frontier with military conflict through 1795.
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers of primarily English, Scots-Irish, German, and Virginia/Pennsylvania origin; significant Native American populations throughout the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker congregations appeared earliest; Catholic presence near French-era settlements. Formal church organization was thin in 1790 — circuit riders and itinerant preachers served scattered settlements rather than established parishes.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); founding of Marietta (1788); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795); Ohio statehood (1803). The active military conflict through 1794 severely limited civilian record-keeping and settlement.

## Boundary changes

This is the most critical factor for 1790 Ohio research. The jurisdictional picture was fluid:

- **1787:** Northwest Territory established — the entire future Ohio fell under a single territorial government with no county subdivisions.
- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county in the Northwest Territory, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River and beyond. All records from Ohio's founding settlements (Marietta, etc.) before 1790 are Washington County records.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized — covering a large portion of southwestern Ohio. An ancestor near Cincinnati after 1790 falls under Hamilton County, not Washington County.
- **1796 and after:** Additional counties were carved rapidly (Adams, Clermont, Fairfield, Trumbull, etc.). County formation accelerated as settlers arrived.
- **1803:** Ohio statehood; the territorial government dissolved and county-level government became the primary record-keeping unit.

**The practical consequence:** An event in "Ohio" in 1790 was recorded — if at all — under Washington County or Hamilton County territorial court records, not under any later county that might cover the same ground today. Always identify which 1788–1803 county held the location before searching records.

The FamilySearch wiki (Ohio Genealogy, "Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes" section, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory) confirms: "Washington County (1788) was the first county organized, followed by Hamilton County (1790). Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus."

### Special land districts — a geographic split within Ohio

Ohio was not surveyed uniformly. Three distinct land systems operated simultaneously, each with its own records held in different repositories:

1. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): Reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans; used a metes-and-bounds survey. Warrants and grants originated in Virginia. Per the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records): "Virginia Military District warrants are at the Virginia State Library."
2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Surveyed on a different grid system. Records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
3. **U.S. Military District** and **Seven Ranges** (federal public land): Administered by the federal government; patents at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) records online.

Which district held a given ancestor's land depends on exactly where within Ohio they settled. These are not temporal splits (before/after a date) — they are geographic splits covering different parts of the state simultaneously. You must know the approximate location before you can identify the correct repository for land records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Ohio did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1790 or at statehood (1803). The FamilySearch wiki's generic guidance confirms that many U.S. states "did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s." The specific Ohio statewide vital registration date is not confirmed by the Ohio-specific wiki pages returned (all resolved to a generic fallback), so a precise year cannot be stated here without risk of error. The FamilySearch Ohio Vital Records page did not return Ohio-specific content in this survey — consult it directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records.
- **What exists for 1787–1810:** No civil vital registration system was in place for the period of interest. The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection ID 1803785; 1,523,678 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) is the earliest available marriage record series and begins in 1789 — this is the primary civil record for marriage in the territorial and early statehood period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; marriages from 1789 onward are digitized and indexed on FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths were not civilly registered in this period at any level. County death records do not begin until 1840 (FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001," collection ID 1417891).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only source for baptisms and burials in this era. See Church Records below.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker; sparse Catholic presence. Formal congregational records are thin for 1790 — circuit riders served most communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; confirmations where congregations were formally organized.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (collection ID 2246917; 678,234 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) is available online. Denominational archives hold originals: Presbyterian records at the Presbyterian Historical Society; Methodist at the United Methodist Archives; Quaker at various meeting archives.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Caveat:** Coverage for 1787–1800 within this collection is likely thin. Formal congregations were few and circuit-rider records irregular. Do not assume a church record exists for this period — verify against the collection's actual date coverage.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census was 1790, but Ohio/Northwest Territory was incompletely enumerated. The region was a frontier with active conflict, and census coverage was sparse. The 1800 federal census is the first with meaningful Ohio coverage.
- **State/territorial census:** No territorial census for Northwest Territory Ohio has been identified in this survey's tool results. The FamilySearch wiki's generic page notes territorial censuses "may fill gaps" but does not confirm one exists for Ohio pre-1803. Consult the Ohio History Connection directly.
- **Access:** The 1800 federal census for Ohio counties is indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court minutes also recorded road assignments, indigent relief, and county business.
- **Date range:** Washington County territorial court records begin 1788; Hamilton County 1790.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch wiki confirms that early court and land records are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory). County courthouses hold later records once counties were formally organized. No FamilySearch indexed collection for territorial-era probate or court records was returned in this survey — treat these as physical-only for 1787–1803 unless confirmed otherwise.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only / microfilm for territorial-era materials; consult the Ohio History Connection.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Three concurrent systems — Virginia Military District (metes and bounds), Connecticut Western Reserve (township grid), and federal rectangular survey (Seven Ranges, U.S. Military District, and other federal tracts). Which applies depends on location within Ohio.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:**
  - Virginia Military District: Virginia State Library holds warrants and grants.
  - Connecticut Western Reserve: Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
  - Federal tracts: Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) at glorecords.blm.gov — searchable online.
  (Source: FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)
- **Types:** Patents, warrants, deeds, grants; tax records (Washington County tax records exist from 1799; FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850," collection ID 1987542, 345,890 records).
- **FamilySearch land collection:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection ID 1542187; 234,567 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) — this is the most directly relevant collection for the 1790 period.
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch land collection is indexed (name-searchable). BLM GLO records are freely searchable online. Virginia Military District records at the Virginia State Library are physical/microfilm.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785–1795), including the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794). The War of 1812 also touched Ohio. Revolutionary War veterans settling in the Virginia Military District generated bounty land warrant records.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (especially relevant for Virginia Military District settlers), and militia muster rolls.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) — pension and bounty land files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for many military records online; state adjutant general records at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Note:** Bounty land warrants for Virginia veterans are at the Virginia State Library, not NARA.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer cemeteries in Marietta (Mound Cemetery, 1788 burials) and Cincinnati area are among the earliest. Many early burials were family plots with no formal sexton records.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage of many Ohio pioneer cemeteries, though completeness for 1787–1810 burials is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare or nonexistent for most locations — formal cemetery administration post-dates most burials of the 1790 period.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, founded 1793) was the first newspaper in the Northwest Territory. The Ohio Gazette (Marietta, 1801) followed near statehood.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and historical society collections. Coverage of 1790s papers in digitized form is limited.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices and obituaries are rare in 1790s frontier papers; legal notices and land sales are more common.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant routes:** Settlers arrived primarily via the Ohio River from Pittsburgh, or overland through Pennsylvania and Virginia. No major seaport border-crossing records apply directly to Ohio.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and naturalization were filed at territorial and county courts (pre-1906, any court of record). No passenger list records apply to inland Ohio. The FamilySearch wiki confirms pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record.
- **Where held:** Territorial court naturalization records at the Ohio History Connection; later county naturalizations at county courthouses.
- **Content note:** Settler arrival in Ohio in the 1790s was overland or by river — passenger manifests do not apply. Focus on court naturalization records and land entry records to establish arrival timing.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial property tax and personal property lists.
- **Date range:** Washington County tax records begin 1799 per the volume search results (FamilySearch digitized volume 005112240, covering 1799–1803, 73 images, 12% name-indexed). FamilySearch also holds "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (collection ID 1987542).
- **Substitute value:** Tax records are critical substitutes for the absent 1790 census data and missing vital records. A person appearing in an 1800 or 1801 tax list confirms presence in a county before the 1800 census. The 1799–1803 Washington County volume is partially indexed (12%) — browse-only for most entries.

### Other record types

- **Territorial land records (Northwest Territory):** FamilySearch digitized volume 005112233 covers Northwest Territory territorial land records 1788–1799 (51 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). This is browse-only and must be examined image by image — one of the few record series that reaches back to 1788.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century county histories for Washington County and Hamilton County frequently transcribed early records (court minutes, land entries, pioneer biographies) that may be the only surviving record of an event. These are major secondary sources for this era.
- **Native American records:** Interactions between settlers and Native peoples (treaty proceedings, land cessions) were recorded by the federal government and are at NARA. These do not directly trace settler families but provide context for why families moved or were displaced.

## Repository guide

| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850 (345,890 records); Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001 (2,156,789 records; postdates this period); Territorial land records 1788–1799 (browse-only, 51 images); Washington County tax records 1799–1803 (partial index, 73 images) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) — 1800 census is the first with Ohio coverage | Subscription |

| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including 1793+ Northwest Territory papers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Ohio pioneer cemeteries | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Pension files, bounty land warrants, territorial records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Ohio for 1780–1810, with a total results count of 2 — this appears to be the complete set of FamilySearch-digitized volumes for this narrow early period, not a truncated page. The collections_search returned 5 collections total for Ohio; all 5 are detailed above.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Early territorial court records (1788–1803); early county records; state archives | In-person; some records online via Ohio Memory |
| Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA | Virginia Military District bounty land warrants and grants | In-person; some digitized |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records; northeastern Ohio materials | In-person; research inquiries |
| NARA, Washington DC / regional | Military pension files, bounty land warrants, territorial records | In-person; microfilm; some online via Fold3 |
| Washington County Courthouse, Marietta | County-level records from 1788 | In-person / mail |
| Hamilton County Courthouse, Cincinnati | County-level records from 1790 | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online

- Territorial court minutes (Washington County 1788–, Hamilton County 1790–): Physical at the Ohio History Connection; not identified as indexed or digitized on FamilySearch in this survey.
- Virginia Military District warrants at the Virginia State Library: physical/microfilm only for most records.
- Pre-1800 church records for most congregations: scattered in denominational archives; not systematically digitized.
- Connecticut Western Reserve land records at the Western Reserve Historical Society: physical.
- Naturalization records from territorial courts: physical at the Ohio History Connection.
- Pioneer cemetery sexton records: rarely survived; physical if they exist at all.

## Known record losses

- The 1790 federal census for the Northwest Territory/Ohio is incomplete or missing. The region was a frontier under active military conflict; enumeration was not thorough. No substitute territorial census has been confirmed by the tools returned in this survey.
- Many early church records were never formally organized — itinerant preachers kept personal registers, some of which were lost when those ministers died or moved on.
- County formation was rapid and records custody was sometimes chaotic. Records created under Washington County jurisdiction (1788) for areas later carved into new counties remained with Washington County rather than transferring — always search Washington County first for 1788–1796 events regardless of what modern county covers the location.

## Research tips

- **Determine the 1788–1803 county before searching.** All Ohio records before 1803 are at the territorial county level, not modern county boundaries. Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790) covered the entire territory between them initially. Per the FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory): "Researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event."
- **Land records reveal settlement earlier than any other source.** For 1790, land entries and warrants are often the first documented evidence of a person's presence in Ohio. Start with "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" and the BLM GLO for federal tracts.
- **The Virginia Military District requires a Virginia search.** If your ancestor settled between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, their land grant originated in Virginia. Search the Virginia State Library for the warrant before looking in Ohio. (Source: FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records.)
- **The Connecticut Western Reserve requires a separate repository.** Northeastern Ohio settlers' land records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland, not at the Ohio History Connection or BLM. (Source: FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records.)
- **Tax lists substitute for the absent 1790 census.** The Washington County tax list begins 1799 and is 12% indexed — browse it image by image for the early years.
- **County histories are essential for this era.** 19th-century histories of Washington and Hamilton counties frequently transcribed territorial court minutes, early land entries, and pioneer biographies. These may be the only surviving record of events from the 1790s. Search WorldCat for titles covering Washington County, Ohio and Hamilton County, Ohio history.
- **The marriage collection reaches back to 1789.** "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (FamilySearch collection 1803785) is indexed and searchable and begins at the territory's founding — check it for early marriages even though no statewide vital registration existed.
- **Assume the 1790 federal census will not include your ancestor.** Coverage in Ohio for 1790 was sparse due to frontier conditions and ongoing warfare. The 1800 census is the first reliable enumeration for most Ohio locations.
- **Browse the territorial land records volume image by image.** FamilySearch volume 005112233 (Northwest Territory, 1788–1799 territorial land records, 51 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be examined page by page.
- **Search adjoining state records.** Families who settled in Ohio in the 1780s–1790s typically came through Pennsylvania and Virginia. Their birth, marriage, and earlier land records may be in those states. The Ohio River corridor means Kentucky records may also be relevant for southwestern Ohio families crossing the river.

---

This guide covers the Northwest Territory / early Ohio period from 1787 (territorial establishment) to approximately 1810, with primary focus on the c. 1790 pre-statehood window. The key research challenge of this period is that Ohio did not exist as a state, counties formed rapidly and changed borders frequently, and civil infrastructure was almost entirely absent — meaning land records and the 1800 census are the primary documentary anchors, supplemented by the earliest county marriage records (from 1789) and whatever church records survive from frontier congregations.

The next step, if you're ready, would be to run a research plan targeting a specific ancestor or family — narrowing to the exact location within Ohio so the correct land district and 1788–1803 county can be identified and the right repositories prioritized.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: California, 1848–1860 (Gold Rush Era)

Here is a comprehensive locality research guide for tracing Gold Rush–era ancestors in California:

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

California was admitted to the Union on **September 9, 1850** as the 31st state, bypassing territorial status. Before statehood it was Mexican Alta California, then under U.S. military governance (1846–1850). Its population exploded from ~14,000 non-Indigenous residents in 1848 to ~300,000 by 1855. The 1850 federal census recorded 92,597 persons — the first federal count in the state.

The state had **27 original counties** at statehood, with boundaries that shifted frequently as mining populations moved. Always verify which county had jurisdiction over a specific mining district at the exact date of the event you are researching.

---

## Key Record Types

### Census Records
- **1850 Federal Census** — *Partially destroyed*. Some county returns are missing — a critical gap. Never assume a missing ancestor wasn't there without verifying which counties' returns survive.
- **1852 California State Census** — The most important source for Gold Rush arrivals, filling the gap between the damaged 1850 and the 1860 federal census. **88% name-indexed and full-text searchable** on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601001). Start here.
- **1860 Federal Census** — First intact federal census for California; captures settlers who arrived during the rush and stayed.
- **Mortality Schedules** (1850 & 1860) — Record deaths in the year preceding the census; vital given high mining-camp mortality from disease, accident, and violence.

### Vital Records (County-Level)
- **County Births, 1850–1919** — FamilySearch collection 2017276; indexed + images.
- **County Marriages, 1850–1952** — FamilySearch collection 1452832; indexed + images.
- **Deaths**: No dedicated indexed FamilySearch collection was found for the 1850s window — a coverage gap. Seek church registers, cemetery records, and newspaper notices instead.
- **Gaps**: Coverage is uneven. Mining camp deaths were frequently unrecorded or found only in church or company registers.

### Church Records
- **Catholic Mission Records, 1769–1850** — FamilySearch collection 1804372; critical for Californio and Indigenous ancestors just before the rush. Records often in Spanish or Latin.
- Catholic diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento) and individual parish offices hold sacramental registers for the 1850s.
- Protestant circuit-rider ministers kept informal registers that may not have survived. Check denominational archives and local historical societies.

### Great Registers (Voter Registration) ⭐ Key Origin Source
- **California Great Registers, 1866–1910** — FamilySearch collection 1923340; 1,345,678 records, indexed + images.
- Although starting in 1866 (outside the core window), these records are *uniquely valuable*: they record each male voter's **name, age, physical description, occupation, country/state of birth, and length of California residence**, allowing you to calculate approximate arrival year and confirm birthplace for a Gold Rush migrant.

### Court, Probate & Naturalization Records
- County probate files for miners who died intestate name heirs and often reveal family relationships and places of origin.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** were filed in *any court of record* — county, district, or federal. Declarations of intention at California county courthouses are a prime source for foreign-born miners' country and town of origin.
- No dedicated indexed FamilySearch collection for California probate files was found; these remain largely physical/microfilm records.

### Land & Mining Claim Records
- **San Francisco Mining Claim Registers, 1849–1855** — FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601002; 340 images. **Browse-only** (0% indexed).
- County recorders throughout the mining counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, etc.) held mining district claim books — contact the county recorder or historical society.
- **BLM General Land Office Records** (federal patents): free at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — more relevant for agricultural settlers than miners.

### Ship Passenger Lists & Arrival Records
- Most sea-route migrants arrived at **San Francisco** (via Panama, Cape Horn, or Pacific routes from China/Australia). Manifests are held physically at **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA**; some are on Ancestry.
- **Sacramento Port Arrival Registers, 1849–1858** — FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601003; 298 images. **Browse-only** (0% indexed).
- Overland migrants left no single arrival record — substitute with trail diaries/journals, and county records from first place of settlement.

### Tax Records
- County assessment rolls (from 1850) can place a miner in a specific county in off-census years and document property (including mining equipment and claims).
- Held at county assessors/archives and the California State Archives. No indexed FamilySearch collection found.

### Newspapers
- **Alta California** (San Francisco, from 1849) and **Sacramento Union** (from 1851) are the major papers.
- Content: obituaries, marriage notices, estate administration notices, mining claim ads, ship arrival notices — all naming individuals.
- **Free online**: California Digital Newspaper Collection at [cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu), including the Alta California.
- **Subscription**: Newspapers.com.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County births, marriages; Great Registers; 1852 State Census; Mission Records; Mining Claim Registers (browse-only); Port Arrivals (browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | Federal censuses (1850, 1860); passenger lists | Subscription |
| **NARA Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA)** | San Francisco ship passenger manifests; federal court naturalizations | In-person; some on Ancestry/FS |
| **California State Archives (Sacramento)** | 1852 State Census; Spanish/Mexican land grant files; state militia; some county records | In-person; some digital |
| **California State Library (Sacramento)** | Newspapers; county histories; periodicals | In-person; some digital |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush diaries/journals; Bancroft settler interviews (unique!) | In-person by appointment |
| **County courthouses & recorder offices** | Deed books; marriage registers; probate files; naturalizations; mining district claim registers | In-person or mail request |
| **California Historical Society (SF)** | Photographs; manuscripts; Gold Rush ephemera | In-person |
| **BLM GLO** | Federal land patents | Free at glorecords.blm.gov |
| **California Digital Newspaper Collection** | Scanned California papers incl. Alta California | Free at cdnc.ucr.edu |

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1850 federal census**: Some county returns destroyed. Verify which counties are missing before concluding an ancestor was absent.
- **Mining camp records**: Many camps were temporary; camp-level records were informal and rarely preserved.
- **Courthouse fires**: Several California counties suffered 19th-century courthouse fires. Verify record survival for your specific county before concluding a record type is absent.

---

## Research Strategy Tips

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601001). This is the single most accessible source for Gold Rush arrivals.

2. **Use the Great Registers for origin research** — Although starting in 1866, they record state/country of birth and length of California residence, letting you calculate approximate arrival year (collection 1923340 on FamilySearch).

3. **Identify the arrival route first**: Sea-route migrants → San Francisco ship manifests; overland migrants → trail diaries, first-settlement county records.

4. **Research at the county level**: Mining claims, probate, naturalizations, and deed records were all created and held at the county level. Identify which county covered the specific mining district, then research that county's records.

5. **For foreign-born miners, seek naturalizations at the county district court** — declarations of intention before 1906 could be filed anywhere, and these are often the best source for country and town of origin.

6. **Check the Bancroft Library's settler interviews** — Hubert Bancroft's organization interviewed hundreds of early California settlers in the 1870s–1880s. These manuscripts often contain detailed biographical information for people who left almost no other surviving record. In-person access at UC Berkeley.

7. **Search the mortality schedules** attached to the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses — high mining-camp mortality makes these schedules a significant finding tool.

8. **Use the Alta California newspaper free at cdnc.ucr.edu** — arrival notices, legal notices, death announcements, and business notices name individuals throughout the Gold Rush period.

---

California in the 1850s means working with brand-new county-level records created from scratch at statehood, partial federal census destruction, and largely unindexed mining-specific records. The 1852 state census and the Great Registers are the two most powerful online starting points. The biggest gap for most researchers is that ship arrival manifests and mining claim registers outside San Francisco remain largely physical records requiring in-person or mail access.
