output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (c. 1860–1885, centered on the 1871 Fire)

## The Record-Loss Problem: What the Fire Destroyed

The destruction of the Cook County Courthouse on October 9–10, 1871 is the defining fact for any Chicago genealogical search in this era. The courthouse held deeds, land records, birth and death registers, court records (including naturalizations), and tax rolls — **all destroyed**. This is not a gap bridgeable by a different database; those originals no longer exist.

The strategy is two-track: (1) use federal records and out-of-courthouse records that survived because they weren't held at the courthouse, and (2) use reconstruction records created after the fire.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Civil registration in Cook County began in 1871. Records surviving from that year onward begin effectively with the *post-fire* period.
- **FamilySearch collections (online, free):**
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940* — 1,450,000 records
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947* — 980,000 records
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920* — 620,000 records
- ⚠️ **Critical gap:** There are no surviving Cook County civil birth or death registrations from before October 1871.

### Church Records
- **The single most important pre-fire substitute.** Church registers kept at the parish — not the courthouse — were more likely to survive.
- **FamilySearch:** *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978)
- **Catholic parishes:** Archdiocese of Chicago's **Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers — contact required for access.
- **Languages:** German, Bohemian/Czech, Norwegian records exist for immigrant-language congregations.
- ⚠️ Parishes *inside* the burn zone lost their registers along with the building. Verify whether a specific parish was in the burn zone before assuming its pre-fire registers are available.

### Census Records
- **1870 federal census survived** — originals were in Washington, DC, not the courthouse. This is the last pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households. Also 1860, 1850, and 1880.
- **Mortality schedules** (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) survived for the same reason.
- **Illinois state censuses** of 1855 and 1865 are at the Illinois State Archives; confirm holdings before searching.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free).

### Probate and Court Records
- **Pre-fire:** Destroyed with the courthouse. Do not expect a surviving pre-fire probate file.
- **Post-fire:** Court and probate records resume after reconstruction; held at **IRAD-NEIU** (Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University).

### Land Records
- **Federal land patents** (pre-courthouse) at [GLO Records](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free, online, and unaffected by the fire.
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Destroyed. However, the **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register their deeds — these reconstructed records survive at the **Cook County Recorder of Deeds**.
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection** at the **Chicago History Museum** contains pre-fire title abstracts and insurance records — one of the most important repositories for pre-fire land research.
- **Digitized volumes on FamilySearch:**
  - Volume 009982110 — 38 images, 1865–1871, "Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)" — **0% indexed, browse-only**
  - Volume 009982111 — 112 images, 1871–1880, "Post-fire Property Re-recordings" — **41% indexed**, remainder browse-only

### Military Records
- Civil War service records and pension files are at NARA — **not held at the courthouse, fully intact**.
- Available on **Fold3** (subscription) and **Ancestry** (subscription).
- Civil War draft registrations (1863) also survived.

### Cemetery Records
- **Graceland Cemetery** (est. 1860), **Rosehill Cemetery** (est. 1859), and **Calvary Catholic Cemetery** were outside the burn zone and their sexton records largely survive.
- **FindAGrave** (free) and **BillionGraves** have substantial Chicago coverage.
- Cemetery records can provide death dates for people whose death certificates were destroyed in the fire.

### Newspaper Records
- The **Chicago Tribune** (founded 1847) resumed publication days after the fire and published extensive survivor lists, relief fund lists, and death notices in October–November 1871.
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) holds historical Tribune issues; **Newberry Library** holds Tribune microfilm.
- **Chicago History Museum** holds clipping files and scrapbooks related to the fire.

### Immigration & Naturalization Records
- **Passenger lists** (federal, held in Washington) survived entirely — available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Pre-fire naturalizations filed in Cook County courts** were destroyed. Check federal district/circuit court records separately at **NARA Great Lakes Region** (Chicago).
- **Post-fire naturalizations** survive at NARA Great Lakes and IRAD.

### Tax Records
- **Pre-fire county tax rolls:** Destroyed.
- **Federal tax assessment lists (1862–1872):** Held in Washington — survived. Available on Ancestry. Lists taxable personal property and income, one of the few tax-era substitutes for the destroyed county records.

### City Directories & Relief Records
- **Chicago city directories (1840s onward):** Survived; held at the **Newberry Library** and digitized on Ancestry. The 1871 edition (pre-fire) and 1872 edition (post-fire) together show who remained in Chicago after the disaster.
- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records:** Named displaced families receiving aid after the fire. Physical records at the **Chicago History Museum** — not digitized, visit or inquiry required.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925; Birth/Death/Marriage records 1871+; 2 digitized volumes of land/court records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1850–1880; federal tax lists 1862–1872; Civil War records; passenger lists; city directories | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records; pension files; military draft records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Chicago Tribune including Oct–Nov 1871 survivor coverage | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Chicago cemetery records | Free |
| GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Illinois | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust title abstracts; Relief and Aid Society lists; fire survivor records; photographs; manuscripts |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories (1840s+); maps; manuscripts; genealogical collections |
| **IRAD-NEIU** (Chicago) | Cook County post-fire court and county records |
| **Archdiocese Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region** (Chicago) | Federal court naturalization records; federal agency records |
| **Cook County Clerk / Recorder of Deeds** | Post-fire vital records; Burnt Record Act re-recordings |
| **Illinois State Archives** (Springfield) | State-level records; some county records |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1870 census.** It is the last pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households and survived because originals were in Washington, DC.

2. **The Burnt Record Act of 1872 is your land-record lifeline.** Combine re-recorded deeds with the Chicago Title and Trust Company abstracts at the Chicago History Museum.

3. **Federal records did not burn.** Civil War service records, pension files, passenger lists, federal tax assessments, and federal court naturalizations are fully intact.

4. **The Chicago Tribune's October–November 1871 survivor and relief coverage** is a primary genealogical source that many researchers overlook.

5. **Church records are the only surviving vital-record substitute for the pre-fire period.** Identify the denomination and specific parish — then check whether that parish was in the burn zone.

6. **City directories pinpoint your ancestor before and after the fire.** The 1871 directory and 1872 directory together show who stayed and who may have relocated.

7. **The Relief and Aid Society records name fire victims and displaced families.** Physical records at the Chicago History Museum; not digitized — visit or written inquiry required.

8. **Do not assume a pre-1871 naturalization in Cook County courts survives.** Search NARA Great Lakes Region for federal court naturalizations filed separately from county courts.

9. **Browse-only volumes require patience.** Volume 009982110 (pre-fire reconstructed court records) is 0% indexed — browse image by image on FamilySearch. Volume 009982111 (post-fire property re-recordings) is only 41% indexed; browse the unindexed portions as well.

---

The key takeaway: researching a Chicago family around 1871 means working around one of the largest genealogical record losses in American history. The good news is that **federal records — censuses, military files, passenger lists, federal tax assessments — all survived intact** because they were never held in Chicago. Church registers, city directories, newspaper survivor lists, and the Relief and Aid Society records fill in much of the rest. The Chicago History Museum and Newberry Library are essential physical repositories for the records that remain.

- **Formed:** Cook County formed 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois
- **Population during period:** Chicago grew from roughly 109,000 (1860 federal census) to 298,977 (1870) and 503,185 (1880) — one of the fastest-growing cities in the country in this period. Population figures are from federal census schedules; the place_population tool did not return data for this standardPlace.
- **Economy:** Railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber, grain trading, manufacturing; the fire destroyed the central business district, prompting massive reconstruction
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, Scandinavian, and Bohemian immigrant communities were well established by 1871; substantial native-born American population as well
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish and German immigrants), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and numerous smaller immigrant-language congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8-10, 1871 — destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed roughly 300 people, left over 100,000 homeless, and consumed the Cook County Courthouse along with most of the city's official pre-fire records

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were largely stable by 1850 and remained so through this period; no significant reorganization affected the jurisdictional chain during 1860-1885.
- The city of Chicago expanded by annexation throughout the 1860s-1880s; neighborhoods annexed after 1871 may have town-level records from their independent period before annexation.

---

## The Record-Loss Problem: What the Fire Destroyed

The destruction of the Cook County Courthouse on October 9-10, 1871 is the defining fact for any Chicago genealogical search in this era. Per the Wikipedia article on the [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the courthouse housed:

- Deeds and land records
- Birth and death registers
- Court records (including naturalizations)
- Tax rolls

All were destroyed. This is not a gap that can be bridged by searching a different database — those specific pre-fire originals no longer exist. The strategy for the 1871 era is therefore a two-track one: (1) use federal records and out-of-courthouse records that survived because they were not held at the courthouse, and (2) use the reconstruction records created after the fire.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Cook County civil registration of births and deaths began in 1871. The records surviving from that year onward begin effectively with the post-fire period, since the courthouse was destroyed in October 1871. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Illinois Vital Records did not load successfully, so I cannot cite a specific statewide registration date from that source; the FamilySearch collection metadata confirms the Cook County series begins 1871.
- **What exists (FamilySearch collections):**

  - Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871-1947 — 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)

- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, free); Cook County Clerk's office holds originals
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the primary substitute for events before 1871 and for the months immediately after the fire. The 1870 federal census (originals held in Washington, DC) survived the fire and gives a household snapshot of pre-fire Chicago families.
- **Critical gap:** There are no surviving Cook County civil birth or death registrations from before October 1871. Do not assume a pre-fire civil registration exists.

### Church records

- **What exists (FamilySearch collection):** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925 — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978). This is the single most important pre-fire source, because church registers kept at the parish rather than the courthouse were more likely to survive.
- **Denominations with records:** Catholic parishes (Irish, German, Bohemian-language), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal. Many immigrant congregations kept registers in their heritage language (German, Norwegian, Bohemian/Czech).
- **Repository for Catholic records:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives — holds Catholic parish registers. Contact required for access. Per the wiki_search result ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)), this is the holding institution.
- **Language note:** German-language parishes kept registers in German; Bohemian/Czech and Norwegian parishes similarly used their heritage language. Researchers must be able to read those records or use a translator.
- **Note on survival:** Not all parish registers survived the fire. Churches in the burned district lost their records along with the building. Parishes outside the burn zone, or those whose registers had been sent to a central archive, have better survival rates. Verify whether a specific parish was in the burn zone before concluding its pre-fire registers are available.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the original schedules were held in Washington, DC — not in the Cook County Courthouse. This is the single most valuable pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households. The 1860 and 1850 censuses also survive. The 1880 census covers the post-fire rebuilt city.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (listing deaths in the year preceding the census) exist for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880. The 1870 mortality schedule covers deaths from June 1869 to May 1870 — before the fire — and survived.
- **Illinois state census:** Illinois conducted state censuses in 1855 and 1865. These are separate from federal census schedules and may be available at the Illinois State Archives; confirm holdings before searching.
- **Access:** Federal census schedules for Illinois are indexed and available on Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). The 1880 census is fully indexed on both.

- **Pre-fire (before October 1871):** Cook County probate files and court records held at the courthouse were destroyed. Researchers should not expect to find an original pre-fire probate file.

- **Post-fire:** Court and probate records resume after the fire. The Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) holds Cook County records from the post-fire period, per the wiki_search result ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal-land (rectangular survey) state; land patents from the federal government are searchable at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov — free, online).
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Original deed books were destroyed in the courthouse fire.
- **Reconstruction — the Burnt Record Act of 1872:** This Illinois law required property owners to re-register their deeds. Reconstructed deed records from this effort survive and are held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds. Per the Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire, these reconstructed deeds are a key substitute source.
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection, held at the Chicago History Museum, contains pre-fire title abstracts and insurance records that document property ownership before 1871. This is one of the most important repositories for pre-fire land research.
- **Two digitized volumes (volume_search):**
  - Volume 009982110 — 38 images, 1865-1871, "Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)." This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image.
  - Volume 009982111 — 112 images, 1871-1880, "Post-fire Property Re-recordings." 41% name-indexed; not full-text searchable — partially searchable by name, remainder browse-only.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861-1865) directly preceded the fire period; many Chicago men served. Veterans were present throughout the 1870s-1880s community.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files are at NARA (National Archives, Washington, DC) and are available via Fold3 (subscription) and Ancestry (subscription). These records were NOT held at the Cook County Courthouse and survived the fire entirely.
- **Draft records:** Civil War draft registrations (1863 Enrollment Act) survived and are available at NARA and on Ancestry/Fold3.
- **Veterans' schedules:** The 1890 federal census is largely destroyed nationwide, but the 1890 Union Veterans Schedule (listing Civil War veterans) has some Illinois survivors — check NARA and Ancestry for Cook County coverage.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (founded 1860), Rosehill Cemetery (founded 1859), and Calvary Catholic Cemetery were all outside the burn zone and their sexton records largely survive.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com, free) has substantial Chicago cemetery coverage. BillionGraves also covers some Chicago cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton record books for surviving cemeteries may be held by the cemetery office or have been microfilmed. Contact individual cemeteries for access.
- **Note:** Cemetery records can provide death dates for people whose death certificates were destroyed in the fire.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune, founded 1847, survived the fire (the Tribune building burned but the paper resumed publication days later). It published extensive survivor lists, relief fund lists, and death notices in October-November 1871. Chicago Inter Ocean and other papers also published fire-related coverage.
- **Value for fire research:** The Tribune's October-November 1871 issues are primary sources for identifying fire victims and survivors. Obituaries, legal notices, and marriage announcements continued throughout the reconstruction period.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds historical Chicago Tribune issues. The Newberry Library holds Tribune microfilm. The Chicago History Museum holds clipping files and scrapbooks related to the fire.
- **Survivor and relief lists:** After the fire, relief organizations published lists of displaced persons receiving aid. These lists name heads of household and sometimes family members. The Chicago History Museum holds these records.

### Immigration and naturalization records

- **Relevant ports:** Chicago-area immigrants arrived chiefly through the Port of New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island); some through New Orleans, Baltimore, or Quebec.
- **Passenger lists:** Federal passenger arrival lists are at NARA and online via Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). These records were held in Washington, not Chicago, and survived the fire completely.
- **Naturalization records (pre-fire):** Naturalizations filed in Cook County courts before October 1871 were destroyed. However, naturalizations were also filed in federal district courts and circuit courts — check those records separately at NARA's Great Lakes Region (Chicago).
- **Naturalization records (post-fire):** New declarations and petitions filed after 1871 survive and are held at NARA Great Lakes and the Illinois Regional Archives Depository.
- **Note on passenger lists:** Full manifest entries list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — always examine the full manifest entry for a family, not just the head of household.

### Tax records

- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls were held at the courthouse and were destroyed.
- **Federal tax records:** Federal tax assessment lists created during the Civil War era (1862-1872) were held in Washington, not Chicago, and survive. These are available on Ancestry and list taxable personal property and income for Chicago residents. This is one of the few tax-era substitutes for the destroyed county tax rolls.
- **Post-fire:** County property tax records resume after reconstruction and are held at the Cook County Assessor's office.

### Other record types

- **City directories:** Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the Newberry Library and digitized on Ancestry. The 1871 and 1872 directories are particularly valuable — the 1871 edition was compiled before the fire, and the 1872 edition shows who remained in Chicago after it. Directory entries give a person's address, occupation, and sometimes employer, placing them in the city in the years between censuses.
- **Relief fund records:** The Chicago Relief and Aid Society distributed relief to fire victims and maintained detailed records of recipients. These records, naming displaced families and individuals, are held at the Chicago History Museum.
- **School records:** Chicago school records may be held by the Chicago Public Schools archives; survival from before 1871 is uncertain.

| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Illinois | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Co. insurance/title records; Relief and Aid Society lists; fire survivor records; photographs; manuscripts | In-person; contact for research inquiries at chicagohistory.org |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s onward); maps; manuscripts; genealogical collections | In-person; some materials online |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) | Cook County post-fire court and county records | In-person; written inquiry |

## Records NOT Online

The following record types exist (at least in part) but are not available in any major online database:

- Chicago Relief and Aid Society lists — physical, at the Chicago History Museum
- Chicago Title and Trust Company pre-fire title abstracts — physical, at the Chicago History Museum
- Post-fire Cook County court records at IRAD-NEIU — not digitized
- Catholic parish registers not microfilmed by FamilySearch — held at the Bernardin Archives or individual parishes
- Chicago school records
- Sexton records for individual cemeteries beyond what FindAGrave has transcribed

---

## Known Record Losses

The single largest record loss in Cook County history was the October 1871 fire destruction of the Cook County Courthouse. Per the [Wikipedia article on the Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the following were destroyed:

- All pre-fire deed books and land records held at the courthouse
- Birth and death registers held at the courthouse
- Court records including pre-fire naturalizations
- Tax rolls

There is no known surviving copy of these records; no microfilm was made before 1871. **The federal census schedules (held in Washington), federal land patents (federal land office), federal tax assessment lists (federal revenue offices), passenger arrival lists (federal), and Civil War military records (federal) all survived because they were never in Chicago.** Church registers kept at the parish — not the courthouse — also survived in many cases, especially for parishes outside the burn zone.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1870 census before anything else.** It is the last pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households and survived because originals were in Washington, DC. It names every household member, ages, birthplaces, and occupations. ([Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))

2. **The Burnt Record Act of 1872 is your land-record lifeline.** Property owners who re-registered their deeds left a paper trail that can partially reconstruct pre-fire ownership chains. Combine this with the Chicago Title and Trust Company abstracts at the Chicago History Museum.

3. **Federal records did not burn.** Civil War service records, pension files, passenger arrival lists, federal tax assessments, and federal court naturalizations were held in Washington or federal regional offices — none were in the courthouse. These are fully intact and are the backbone of research for the 1860s-1870s.

4. **The Chicago Tribune survivor and relief coverage from October-November 1871** is a primary genealogical source that many researchers overlook. Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library hold microfilm copies.

5. **Church records are the only surviving vital-record substitute for the pre-fire period.** Identify the denomination and, if possible, the specific parish your family attended. Check whether that parish was in the burn zone. The Archdiocese Bernardin Archives and the FamilySearch Cook County Church Records collection (1833-1925, 285,000 records) are the starting points.

6. **City directories pinpoint your ancestor before and after the fire.** The Newberry Library holds Chicago directories from the 1840s onward. The 1871 directory (compiled before the fire) and the 1872 directory (post-fire) together show who was in Chicago and who may have relocated after the disaster.

7. **The Relief and Aid Society records name fire victims and displaced families.** These physical records at the Chicago History Museum have not been digitized; a visit or inquiry is required.

8. **Do not assume a pre-1871 naturalization in Cook County courts survives.** They burned with the courthouse. Search NARA Great Lakes Region for federal court naturalizations, which were filed in separate federal court records that are more likely to have survived.

9. **Browse-only volumes require patience.** Volume 009982110 (pre-fire reconstructed court records, 1865-1871) is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image on FamilySearch. Volume 009982111 (post-fire property re-recordings, 1871-1880) is 41% indexed, so name searching will miss roughly 60% of the entries; browse the unindexed portions as well.

---

No research.json was found at the workspace path, so this guide is presented as a standalone response and no locality entry has been persisted.

---

Researching ancestors in Chicago around 1871 means working around one of the largest genealogical record losses in American history: the destruction of the Cook County Courthouse and virtually every local record it held. The good news is that several major record types survived because they were never in Chicago to begin with — federal census schedules (including the 1870 Chicago census), Civil War military records and pensions, passenger arrival lists, and federal tax assessments are all intact and online. For the years immediately before and after the fire, church registers (held at parishes, not the courthouse), city directories at the Newberry Library, newspaper survivor lists in the Chicago Tribune, and the Chicago Relief and Aid Society records at the Chicago History Museum fill in what the courthouse records cannot. Property researchers have the Burnt Record Act re-recordings and the Chicago Title and Trust Company abstract collection to work with.

The next step is to identify which specific family members you are tracing, confirm whether they were in Chicago in the 1870 census, and then work systematically through the surviving federal records and church series before turning to the physical repositories in Chicago.

Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1762, with Spanish period context to 1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Established:** France claimed the territory in 1682; permanent settlement began in 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718, and served as the administrative center.
- **Administered as:** New France (French crown) 1699–1762 → Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, effective 1769) → briefly France 1800–1803 → United States (Louisiana Purchase, 1803).
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian (Cajun) settlers (arriving post-1755 exile), German Coast settlers, enslaved Africans, Indigenous peoples, and later Canary Island Islanders (Isleños).
- **Religion:** Roman Catholicism exclusively — the only legally recognized church under the Code Noir.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **1699–1762:** Organized into "postes" (military posts/settlements), not counties. The Superior Council governed from New Orleans.
- **1762:** France ceded the colony — split between Spain (west of Mississippi) and Britain (east of Mississippi/Gulf Coast).
- **1769–1803:** Spanish colonial administration. The Superior Council replaced by the Cabildo; records shift to Spanish conventions, though French-language records persist.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase → Territory of Orleans → State of Louisiana (1812).

> **Key researcher note:** Treat the French period (1699–1762) and Spanish period (1769–1803) as two separate administrative jurisdictions with overlapping record series.

---

## Primary Record Types

### Church / Sacramental Records (The Backbone)
- **Why critical:** No civil vital registration existed during the French colonial period. Catholic sacramental registers ARE the birth, marriage, and death records.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" — collection 1612905 (~987,654 records, ~493,827 images). Earliest records from 1718/1720.
- **Digitized Volume:** 004330991 — 264 images, Orleans Parish 1720–1803, Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers. **Browse-only (0% name-indexed).** Language: French and Spanish.
- **Where held (originals):** St. Louis Cathedral / Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.
- **Tip:** Baptism entries often name the enslaver (for enslaved persons), parents, and godparents — making them rich sources for multiple families simultaneously.

### Superior Council & Notarial Records
- **Why critical:** Estate inventories, land concessions, court proceedings, and contracts naming individuals and revealing family relationships — equivalent to court, probate, and land records combined.
- **Digitized Volume:** 004330992 — 149 images, Louisiana statewide 1699–1769, French colonial notarial acts. **Browse-only (0% name-indexed).** Language: French and Spanish.
- **Where held (originals):** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans).
- **Key tip:** Marriage contracts (contrats de mariage) drawn before weddings typically name both parties' parents, their places of origin in France, and property details — often richer than the church register entry itself.

### Notarial Acts (New Orleans Notarial Archives)
- **Oldest continuous notarial office in North America** — acts from the 1730s onward.
- Contains marriage settlements, property sales, wills, and contracts.
- **Access:** In-person at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. Largely not digitized for online researchers.

### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" — collection 2078341 (~456,789 records, ~228,394 images). The 1756–1762 portion covers the late French colonial period.
- Estate inventories often list enslaved persons individually by first name, African origin, and sometimes age — a key African American genealogy source.

### Colonial Census Rolls (Recensements)
- France conducted periodic recensements naming heads of household with family composition and land holdings.
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Also some holdings at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Not digitized** for online search. Largely physical-only for U.S.-based researchers.

### Land Records
- French long lots (arpent system) — narrow strips perpendicular to waterways, not the rectangular U.S. survey system.
- **Post-Purchase confirmations** of colonial land grants: Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge); American State Papers: Public Lands (free online via Library of Congress).
- **Colonial-era grants:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for records made in France.

### Immigration Records
- **Acadian exile lists** (1755 expulsion onward): ANOM; Centre d'études acadiennes (Université de Moncton, New Brunswick, Canada); published in Arsenault's *Histoire et généalogie des Acadiens* and White's *Dictionnaire généalogique des familles acadiennes*.
- **Slave ship records:** Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database — [slavevoyages.org](https://slavevoyages.org) (free, online).
- No regular newspaper was published in French Louisiana during the French period (earliest Louisiana newspaper: 1794).

### Military Records
- French colonial garrison records and muster rolls of the *Compagnies Franches de la Marine*.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence). Spanish-period militia lists at the Louisiana Historical Center.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Collections 1612905 (church records) and 2078341 (probate); browse-only volumes 004330991 and 004330992 | Free |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records 1699–1769; Cabildo records 1769–1803 | In-person or correspondence |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s (marriage contracts, sales, wills) | In-person; public access |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Original sacramental registers; burial records | Contact in advance; restricted |
| **ANOM** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Colonial administrative records, recensements, military records, emigration files | In-person or written correspondence |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge) | Post-1803 confirmations of colonial grants | In-person; American State Papers free online |
| **Centre d'études acadiennes** (Moncton, Canada) | Acadian genealogical records and exile lists | In-person; some published resources online |
| **slavevoyages.org** | Trans-Atlantic slave trade records | Free online |

---

## Known Record Losses & Gaps

- Superior Council records suffered some losses during colonial administration; survival is uneven for settlements outside New Orleans.
- ANOM, New Orleans Notarial Archives, and colonial census rolls are largely physical-only — no significant online name-indexed database.
- The earliest period (1699–1718, before New Orleans was founded) has the thinnest record survival.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with FamilySearch's church records** (collection 1612905), then browse volume 004330991 (1720–1803) for your family's parish.
2. **Browse the Superior Council acts** in volume 004330992 (1699–1769) for legal, land, and estate records.
3. **Pursue notarial marriage contracts** at the New Orleans Notarial Archives — they frequently name parents and French places of origin.
4. **For Acadian ancestors:** The research trail leads to Canada and France first. Exhaust the Moncton archives and published Acadian genealogies before focusing solely on Louisiana records.
5. **For French-origin settlers:** ANOM "Dossiers personnels" and emigration files can name a settler's home village in France, opening the trail back to French parish registers.
6. **You must read 18th-century French script.** Neither FamilySearch volume is name-indexed. A professional translator/paleographer familiar with colonial Louisiana documents is strongly recommended if you don't read French.
7. **The Code Noir creates African American records.** Baptisms of enslaved persons appear in the same sacramental registers as free persons, with the enslaver named — one of the richest pre-1800 sources in North America for this research.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1762, with Spanish period context to 1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Established:** France claimed the territory in 1682; permanent settlement began in 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718. The colony was administered as part of New France under a Superior Council (Conseil Superieur).
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (from 1718)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French crown) 1699–1762; then Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762, formally administered from 1769); briefly retroceded to France 1800–1803; sold to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period. Colonial-era census rolls (recensements) held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France provide some population data.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, indigo and tobacco cultivation, and later sugar production; river commerce along the Mississippi.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Canadien (Acadian) settlers (arriving in force post-1755 expulsion from Acadia), German settlers on the "German Coast" above New Orleans, enslaved Africans, and Indigenous peoples. Spanish settlers and administrators arrived after 1769.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana. The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons.
- **Key historical events:** French settlement 1699; New Orleans founded 1718; Louisiana ceded to Spain 1762 (effective 1769); Acadian exile and arrival 1755–1785; Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes

- **1699–1762:** Louisiana was French colonial territory, administered from New Orleans through the Superior Council. No county system existed; territory was organized into "postes" (military posts and settlements).
- **1762:** France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi River to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau). France also ceded its eastern portions (present-day Alabama/Mississippi coast) to Britain. Records from the period before 1769 (the year Spain effectively took administrative control) continue under the Superior Council's structure.
- **1769–1803:** Spanish colonial administration. The Superior Council was replaced by the Cabildo. Record-keeping shifted to Spanish notarial and ecclesiastical conventions, though French and mixed-language records persisted in practice.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase. U.S. Territory of Orleans created, becoming the State of Louisiana in 1812.
- **Researchers must treat the French period (1699–1762) and Spanish period (1769–1803) as two separate administrative jurisdictions with partially overlapping record series.** Records for the same family may appear in French-language Superior Council acts and later in Spanish-language Cabildo records. The New Orleans notarial office is the continuous thread.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil vital registration during the French colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey and do not state a specific colonial-era civil registration date — no date is asserted here from memory.
- **What exists for the colonial period:** Catholic sacramental registers are the functional equivalent. FamilySearch holds a collection titled "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images). The earliest records begin in 1718, corresponding to the founding of New Orleans and St. Louis Cathedral.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) holds registers from 1720. The Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives holds the original registers. FamilySearch has digitized a portion (see volume 004330991 below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** The sacramental registers ARE the primary birth/marriage/death record for this entire period. Supplement with Superior Council estate records and notarial acts.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholicism exclusively (by law under the Code Noir). No Protestant churches functioned legally in French Louisiana.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons by name), marriages (including details on parents, witnesses, and sometimes origin), burials.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Volume 004330991 — 264 images, covering Orleans Parish 1720–1803, Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers. Languages: French and Spanish. **Digitization level: Browse-only images — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** The researcher must browse image by image and read French (and later Spanish) handwriting directly.
- **Where held:** Original registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; microfilm and digital images via FamilySearch. The FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Genealogy" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)) identifies St. Louis Cathedral records from 1720.
- **Language:** French for the French period (1699–1762); French and Spanish for the Spanish period (1769–1803). Researchers must read 18th-century French script and Latin formulaic phrases used in sacramental entries.

### Census records
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** France conducted periodic recensements (census rolls) of the colony. These are not U.S. federal census records. They name heads of household with household composition and sometimes land holdings. Held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France. The FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Genealogy" identifies ANOM as holding administrative correspondence and census rolls. The Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans also holds some colonial-era enumerations.
- **U.S. federal census:** Louisiana first appeared in the federal census in 1810, well after the colonial period ends. Not applicable to the 1700s.
- **State census:** Not applicable during the colonial period.
- **Access:** ANOM records are largely physical-only for U.S.-based researchers; some finding aids are online at archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr. No FamilySearch-indexed collection was returned for colonial census rolls in this survey.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, successions, guardianship appointments, civil suits, contracts — all processed through the Superior Council (French period) and later the Cabildo (Spanish period).
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Volume 004330992 — 149 images, covering Louisiana statewide 1699–1769, described as "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)." Languages: French and Spanish. **Digitization level: Browse-only images — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image in French.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images). Date range begins 1756 and overlaps the late French colonial period. This is the most accessible collection for late-colonial probate.
- **Where held (originals):** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) — identified by the FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Genealogy" as holding Superior Council records, partially digitized. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial acts from the 1730s onward (see Land Records below).
- **Note:** Estate inventories from this period often name enslaved people individually by first name, African origin, and sometimes age — an important source for African American genealogy.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long lots (arpent system) — narrow strips running perpendicular to the river or bayou, not the rectangular survey system used in most of the U.S.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The French crown granted concessions through the Superior Council; later the Spanish crown through the Cabildo. The FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Land and Property" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)) identifies the American State Papers: Public Lands series and the Louisiana State Land Office as holding documentation of colonial grants as confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish grants, notarial contracts (ventes, echanges, obligations), marriage contracts (contrats de mariage — critical for family relationships), and post-Purchase confirmations.
- **Notarial Archives:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds acts from the 1730s onward and is described in the FamilySearch Wiki as "the oldest continuous notarial office in North America." Marriage settlements, property sales, wills, and contracts are here. Public access is provided.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge) for post-Purchase confirmations of colonial grants; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center for original notarial acts; ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for administrative land grant records made in France.
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch volume 004330992 covers Superior Council notarial-type acts through 1769 — browse-only. The Notarial Archives Research Center is largely physical-only for online researchers.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of Spanish Succession (background); French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754–1763) — directly affected the colony's transfer; American Revolutionary War (Louisiana under Spain supported American patriots); various conflicts with Indigenous peoples and Britain.
- **Record types:** French colonial garrison records, muster rolls of the Compagnies Franches de la Marine (the colonial troops). Spanish militia rolls after 1769.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) holds French colonial military records. The Louisiana Historical Center holds some Spanish-period militia lists. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Military Records returned only generic content in this survey; specific colonial-era military holdings are not confirmed from that page.
- **Access:** ANOM — largely physical-only or via correspondence; some finding aids online. Fold3.com lists military records but returned only generic coverage for this period in this survey.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial-era burials:** Burial entries in the Catholic sacramental registers (volume 004330991, 1720–1803) are the primary record. Physical cemeteries from this period include St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (est. 1789, late colonial/Spanish period). Earlier French-period burials predate formal cemetery establishment.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have minimal coverage for 18th-century Louisiana burials; above-ground tombs were not standardized until later. Rely on the sacramental registers.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the colonial period, where they survive, are held at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Colonial Louisiana:** No regular newspaper was published in French Louisiana during the French colonial period. The first Louisiana newspaper (Le Moniteur de la Louisiane) appeared in 1794 during the Spanish period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries and the New Orleans Public Library hold microfilm of early Louisiana newspapers.
- **Content value:** Not applicable as a colonial-era genealogical source for the 1700s (French period). Obituaries and legal notices begin only in the 1790s.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant arrivals:** French settlers (early 1700s); German Coast settlers (ca. 1720s); Acadian exiles arriving in waves 1755–1785; enslaved Africans (transatlantic slave trade, recorded in ship manifests and at the port). Spanish settlers from the Canary Islands (Islenhos) arrived ca. 1779.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial arrivals are fragmentary. The most genealogically useful are the Acadian exile lists (compiled by French and British authorities during the 1755 expulsion and subsequent migrations), held partly at ANOM and partly at Canadian archives. Slave ship records are documented in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org), a free online resource.
- **Where held:** ANOM holds much of the French colonial emigration paperwork. The U.S. National Archives (NARA) holds post-1803 immigration records. The Centre d'etudes acadiennes at the Universite de Moncton (New Brunswick, Canada) is the primary repository for Acadian records.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable in the colonial period; French and Spanish colonial subjects did not naturalize in the modern sense.

### Tax records
- **Colonial period:** No systematic tax record series equivalent to Anglo-American property tax lists was created under French colonial administration. The closest substitutes are the recensements (census rolls with property listed) and notarial inventories.
- **Spanish period:** The Cabildo maintained some administrative taxation records after 1769. These are held at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Substitute value:** Use the recensements at ANOM and notarial estate inventories as substitutes.

### Other record types

**Superior Council and Cabildo minutes:** These are the colonial government's administrative records — court proceedings, contracts, regulations, lists of settlers, appointments, and estate matters. The Superior Council records (1699–1769) are the single most important non-church source for French colonial families. Held at the Louisiana Historical Center; partially digitized as volume 004330992 on FamilySearch (browse-only, French, 149 images covering 1699–1769).

**Notarial acts:** Marriage contracts (contrats de mariage) were commonly drawn up before marriages in French legal tradition. They name the parties, their parents, their origins, and property arrangements — often the richest single document for a colonial-era family. At the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center from the 1730s onward.

**Code Noir records:** The Code Noir required baptism, marriage, and Christian burial for enslaved people. This means enslaved individuals appear by first name (and sometimes African origin) in the sacramental registers and estate inventories — making colonial Louisiana one of the richer environments in North America for pre-1800 African American genealogical research.

**Local and county histories:** Published 19th- and early-20th-century histories of Louisiana parishes (the equivalent of counties) often reprint colonial-era records and list founding families. The Louisiana State Library and LSU Libraries hold extensive collections.

---

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist but have no significant online database coverage for the French colonial period:

- ANOM recensements (colonial census rolls) — physical-only at Aix-en-Provence
- ANOM military/administrative correspondence — physical-only
- New Orleans Notarial Archives acts prior to any partial digitization — largely physical-only
- Cabildo administrative minutes (Spanish period) — held at Louisiana Historical Center; largely physical or microfilm-only
- Acadian exile lists (detailed emigration records) — held at ANOM, Moncton, and various Canadian archives; some published transcriptions, not fully online

---

## Known record losses

- The Superior Council records suffered some losses during colonial administration. The FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Genealogy" notes partial digitization, implying incompleteness.
- Louisiana's system of ecclesiastical parishes (not civil parishes) means some outlying settlements had infrequent or informal record-keeping before civil parish courts were established after 1807.
- No major courthouse-fire record loss (comparable to Virginia's burned courthouses) is documented for the colonial period specifically, but survival is uneven for records outside New Orleans.

---

## Research tips

- **Catholic sacramental registers are the backbone.** For the French colonial period, all genealogical vital data runs through the Catholic Church. Begin with the FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) and the digitized volume 004330991 (1720–1803, browse-only). The FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Genealogy" at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) identifies St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 as the primary source.
- **The Superior Council records are indispensable for non-vital data.** Estate inventories, land concessions, court proceedings, and contracts in volume 004330992 (1699–1769) and at the Louisiana Historical Center name individuals and reveal family relationships. These must be browsed in French, not searched by name.
- **Notarial marriage contracts often contain more than sacramental registers.** The marriage contract typically names both parties' parents, their places of origin in France, and property details — far richer than the church register entry. At the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center from the 1730s. The FamilySearch Wiki article "Louisiana Land and Property" at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) discusses the notarial archive as the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.
- **For Acadian ancestry, the research trail leads to Canada and France.** The Acadian exile records predate Louisiana arrival. Exhaust the Centre d'etudes acadiennes resources and published Acadian genealogies (Bona Arsenault's "Histoire et genealogie des Acadiens" and Stephen White's "Dictionnaire genealogique des familles acadiennes") before focusing solely on Louisiana records.
- **For French-origin settlers, ANOM is the origin repository.** The "Dossiers personnels" and emigration files at ANOM can name a settler's village of origin in France, opening the trail back to French parish registers. Contact ANOM before planning a visit.
- **Records are in 18th-century French script (and later Spanish).** Researchers who do not read French will need a professional translator or paleographer familiar with colonial Louisiana documents. Latin formulaic entries appear in sacramental registers. Do not rely on automated translation for handwritten records.
- **The Code Noir creates African American genealogical records.** Baptisms of enslaved persons appear in the same sacramental registers as free persons, with the enslaver named. Estate inventories (Superior Council records) list enslaved people individually. This is one of the richest pre-1800 sources in North America for African American family research.
- **The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** (collection 2078341) overlaps the very late French colonial period. Probate records from 1756–1762 were filed under French colonial authority.
- **Do not confuse civil parishes with ecclesiastical parishes.** Louisiana's civil parishes (established after statehood in 1812) do not correspond to the French colonial ecclesiastical parishes. Civil parish boundaries shift; ecclesiastical parish registers are what matter for the 1700s.
- **Naming customs:** French colonial families followed Catholic naming conventions, commonly using the names of saints. Children were often given the same name as a godparent. The same given name reused across generations is the norm, not an exception — distinguish individuals by date, sponsor names, and parents named in the entry. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Naming Customs returned only generic content in this survey; the above reflects the general French Catholic tradition documented in the Wikipedia article on French Louisiana.
- **Research recommended sequence:** (1) FamilySearch "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (indexed); (2) browse volume 004330991 (sacramental registers 1720–1803); (3) browse volume 004330992 (Superior Council acts 1699–1769); (4) FamilySearch "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"; (5) New Orleans Notarial Archives (in-person or correspondence); (6) Louisiana Historical Center (Superior Council originals); (7) ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for origin documentation.

Both are available on FamilySearch in digitized but unindexed image volumes — meaning you must scroll through images and read 18th-century French handwriting directly, with no name search available. The colonial administrative records held in France at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, and the notarial archives in New Orleans, are the key physical repositories that have not been digitized or indexed for online search.

The recommended next step is to identify which specific parish or settlement your ancestor was associated with, then focus the search on the corresponding sacramental register within FamilySearch volume 004330991, followed by the Superior Council notarial acts in volume 004330992.

## Two Colonies, Not One — The Critical First Step

Before 1691, **Plymouth Colony** (Pilgrims, 1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (Puritan Great Migration, 1628/1630) were entirely separate jurisdictions with separate court systems, records, and archives. You must identify which colony your ancestor lived in before searching records:

- **Plymouth Colony** ancestors: Search Nathaniel Shurtleff's published *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (12 volumes) and Plymouth County repositories
- **Massachusetts Bay** ancestors: Search the Massachusetts Archives and county-level records

The two merged into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691**.

---

## Key Record Types and Where to Find Them

### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- Mandated at the **town level** from **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration systems in North America
- **Best starting point:** FamilySearch [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — indexed with images, free
- The published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series (Tanner–Corbin) abstracts town clerk records for 200+ towns; widely available at libraries and NEHGS
- **Important:** Town clerk birth entries and Congregational church baptism records are *separate* — search both

### Church Records (Congregational / Puritan)
- The established church kept membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications can be genealogically rich!)
- FamilySearch [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — indexed with images, free
- A full-text searchable (not name-indexed) volume of Suffolk County Congregational records 1630–1700 exists on FamilySearch (image group 007612045)

### Probate and Court Records
- County-level probate begins **1635** (Essex County among the earliest)
- FamilySearch [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- Colony-level **General Court records** begin 1630 at the Massachusetts Archives — these name ordinary colonists in petitions, land disputes, and disciplinary matters
- ⚠️ Before 1643, county courts didn't exist — search colony-level General Court records only

### Land Records
- Colony → town proprietors granted lots; county deed registries begin **1643**
- Town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 are digitized on FamilySearch (image group 007612044) but **browse-only** (no index, no full-text search)
- Held at County Registries of Deeds and Massachusetts Archives

### Census Substitutes (No colonial census exists)
- **Freemen's lists**, colony/town **rate (tax) lists**, and **militia rolls** are the primary substitutes
- These begin in the 1630s and are held at the Massachusetts Archives; many published in town histories

### Military Records
- Pequot War (1636–1638), King Philip's War (1675–1676)
- Muster rolls, service lists, and relief records at the **Massachusetts Archives** and published in the *Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors* series

### Immigration Records
- Passenger lists for the Great Migration (1620–1643) are **fragmentary** — not all ships have surviving manifests
- ⭐ **The NEHGS Great Migration Study** (AmericanAncestors.org, subscription) is the single most important resource — it reconstructs arrivals from church, court, and deed records with full citations

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records — all indexed + free | Free |
| **AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS)** | Great Migration Study, NEHGR journal, manuscript genealogies | Subscription |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colony records, General Court, probate originals, militia records | In-person |
| **County Courthouses** | Deeds and probate from 1643 | In-person; many filmed by FamilySearch |
| **Individual Town Halls** | Town clerk vital records, meeting minutes | In-person |
| **FindAGrave** | Colonial burial ground transcriptions | Free |

---

## Critical Research Tips

1. **Start with the Great Migration Study** (AmericanAncestors.org) for any immigrant arriving 1620–1643 — it saves enormous time by combining all indirect evidence in one place.

2. **Old Style (Julian) calendar warning:** In the 1600s, the new year began March 25, not January 1. A date recorded as "10 February 1661" actually means what we'd call February 10, 1662. Write dates as "1661/62" to avoid errors.

3. **Records before 1643 are colony-level only** — county courts didn't exist yet.

4. **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** destroyed several western towns (Deerfield, Brookfield); records for those communities may be fragmentary or lost.

5. **Check adjacent colonies** — Connecticut and Rhode Island are nearby, and border families generated records on both sides.

---

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700, Early Puritan Settlement)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628 and settled 1630. Merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Suffolk County, established 1643)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; colonial charter authority
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration (1630–1643) per Wikipedia.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, fur trade, timber, maritime trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) established church; Quakers, Baptists, Anglicans appear by late century
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (1630–1643); four original counties formed 1643; King Philip's War (1675–1676); Salem witch trials (1692)

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony were separate jurisdictions until 1691.
- Original four counties (Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, Norfolk) established 1643. Before 1643, all records are colony-level at the Massachusetts Archives.
- Plymouth Colony had its own county structure from 1685.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording mandated from 1639 (town level, not county or colony-wide)
- **What exists:** Town clerk registers of births, marriages, and deaths from 1639; Plymouth Colony equivalent from 1620
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2061550 (indexed + images); individual town halls; Massachusetts Archives; Tanner-Corbin published series
- **Gaps:** Compliance varied by town; records before a town's incorporation are absent

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (established); Quakers (documented in court records); Baptists and Anglicans late century
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1921657 (indexed + images); Suffolk County Congregational records image group 007612045 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed); Colonial Society of Massachusetts publications; NEHGS
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- No federal census until 1790. Use freemen's lists, tax/rate lists, and militia rolls as substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- **Date range:** 1635 onward (county level from 1643; colony level before)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 (indexed + images); Massachusetts Archives; Plymouth Colony records in Shurtleff's 12-volume published set

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Types:** Town land grants, proprietors' records (browse-only image group 007612044, 188 images, no index), county deeds from 1643
- **Where held:** County Registries of Deeds; Massachusetts Archives; town halls

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638), King Philip's War (1675-1676)
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; published compilations (Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors series)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com)
- **Physical records:** Association for Gravestone Studies transcription projects

### Immigration records
- **Key resource:** NEHGS Great Migration Study (AmericanAncestors.org) for 1620-1643
- **Note:** FamilySearch collection 1784312 (Passenger Lists) covers only 1820-1891 — NOT colonial period

### Tax records
- Colony and town rate lists from 1630s; freemen's lists as census substitute
- Held at Massachusetts Archives; many published in local histories

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |

| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (2061550); Church Records 1630-1920 (1921657); Probate Records 1635-1991 (1678901); browse volumes | Free |
